correctness.rationale: Reconstructed the finite-period normalization: the joint divisibility mean is 1/lcm(d,e), so expanding gcd(d,e) as a sum of totients gives the exact second moment Σ_{r≤By} φ(r)G(r/y)²/r². The first moment is v+O(1/y) by harmonic sums, with no rational-endpoint requirement. Summatory φ and partial summation give κ log x+O(1) for total weight and log(v/u) times κ as the limiting weight of each interval (u,v] away from zero. Finitely many floor jumps on any truncated interval allow integration against the limit. G(t)=v+O(t); for nonzero v the replacement by v² in the second moment costs O(1), since φ(r)/r²≤1/r. For zero v the contribution r≤εy is O(ε²) uniformly, giving exactly the stated finite integral after subtracting the vanishing squared mean. Polarization supplies the rank-one covariance matrix. Direct finite-X pair discrepancies sum to O(y²/X), and the corresponding means cost O(y/X). For the balanced dyadic difference G=−1 on (2,4), proving strict positivity. An independent step-sum calculation with x=4/t and cut at x=400000 gives 0.50821852788883831499…; the omitted positive tail is bounded by 5×10^(−9) using |G(t)|≤10t near zero. Replay: python3 /workspace/branches/f2242719-5199-4216-880c-d47ecbdc3d65/dyadic_constant_decimal_check.py (also dyadic_constant_independent.py). Ford's presence estimate transfers to period sampling by taking X an arbitrarily large multiple of L_y for each fixed y, so each dyadic presence probability tends to zero. The union bound gives convergence in probability to zero for the difference, while its squared mean tends to zero and its second moment does not.
